back: Giant ionic (NaCl, MgO); simple molecular (I₂, C₆₀); hydrogen-bonded (ice); giant molecular (diamond, graphite, SiO₂, Si); giant metallic (Cu).

front: Why do simple molecular solids have low melting points?
back: Only weak intermolecular forces between molecules are overcome; covalent bonds within molecules do not break.

front: Why is diamond hard and non-conducting?
back: Each C bonded tetrahedrally to four others in a giant network; all electrons in localised bonds.

front: Why is graphite soft but conducting?
back: Layers held by weak forces slide; one delocalised electron per C moves along the layers.
Giant covalent: each Si bonded to four O, each O to two Si (tetrahedral network).

front: What is needed for electrical conduction?
back: Mobile charged particles: delocalised electrons (metals, graphite) or free ions (molten / aqueous ionic compounds).

front: Why do ionic compounds often dissolve in water?
back: Polar water molecules are attracted to the ions and surround them (hydration).
The direct change of a solid into a gas (e.g. iodine, solid CO₂).
